opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a pretty dark period. From the outside it looked like everything was going well. I was at MIT, publishing papers, working on Taichi. But inside I felt stuck. A lot of research felt like optimizing for the next paper deadline, and I kept asking myself, "Is this actually what I want to spend my life on?" At some point I seriously thought about just leaving.

A few things helped me see a way forward.

The first was talking to people. I'd kept a lot of it to myself, which made it worse. When I finally opened up to my advisor, friends, and family, I realized I wasn't the only one who felt this way. Many PhD students go through it. Just knowing that took some of the pressure off. It wasn't that I was broken. It was a normal, hard phase.

The second was reconnecting with *why* I started. What really excited me was never the paper count. It was building tools that let people create things that were impossible before. Taichi came out of that. When I focused on making Taichi useful to real users, seeing people around the world use it for simulations, art, and teaching, I started to feel meaning again. The feedback from the community was very energizing.

The third was giving myself permission to define success my own way. I didn't have to follow the standard path of more papers, then a faculty job. Once I accepted that my goal could be building an open-source project and maybe a company around it, the PhD stopped feeling like a cage. It became a place to build something I cared about. So I decided to finish, but on my own terms.

Looking back, my advice is this. When you're unhappy, don't just push through blindly, and don't make a huge decision in the worst moment either. Step back, talk to people you trust, and figure out what actually gives you energy. Then adjust your path toward that. Sometimes the answer is to leave. For me, the answer was to change *how* I was doing it, not *whether* I was doing it.

r001.rationale: He says he was publishing papers and working on Taichi at MIT while feeling stuck and seriously considering leaving.

r002.rationale: He mentions talking to his advisor, but does not identify switching advisors within MIT as an alternative to dropping out.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that pulled me out of it was realizing I didn't have to choose between research and building something people could actually use. For a long time at MIT I felt stuck in this loop where I'd spend months on a paper, it would get reviewed by three people, and then it would basically sit there. I was asking myself, what is this all for? That's when the dropping-out thoughts started.

What changed was Taichi. I started writing this little compiler for computer graphics simulation, mostly because I was frustrated with how painful it was to write high-performance code for my own research. And then I open-sourced it, and people I had never met started using it, filing issues, sending pull requests. Someone in another country would build something cool with it and post it online. That feedback loop was so much faster and more real than the academic one. It made me feel like my work mattered to someone outside my advisor's group.

And the second thing was my advisor, Fredo Durand, and also Bill Freeman. They were surprisingly supportive of me spending time on an open-source project that wasn't obviously going to produce papers. They basically said, if this is what gives you energy, go do it, and the research will follow. And it did. Taichi became the core of my thesis.

So I'd say the lesson for me was that the unhappiness wasn't really about MIT or research itself. It was about not seeing impact. Once I found a channel where I could see people using what I built, everything else, including the PhD, suddenly made sense again. I didn't need to quit. I needed to find my own way of doing it.

r001.rationale: He describes continuing research at MIT while unhappy and says Taichi became the core of his thesis.

r002.rationale: He mentions supportive advisors, but does not identify switching advisors as an alternative to dropping out.

astra-6.text: What helped was stepping back and asking myself what I actually wanted to spend my time doing. When you’re unhappy, it’s easy to focus on what you want to leave. The harder question is what you want to move toward. I didn’t need to figure out my whole future at once. I needed to find a next step that I felt curious and excited about, rather than stay on a path just because it was prestigious.

sol-6.1.text: What helped was separating two questions: was I unhappy with the situation I was in, or did I no longer enjoy the work itself? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing. That gave me a way to think about moving forward without making the whole decision simply “stay at MIT or drop out.”
